Title: First Shift on the Spark Cluster
What the shift is: The cluster is already up. Record the master, how many workers are alive, and the application id of dispatch-stream. Stop leftover scratch. Leave sales-nightly and dispatch-stream alone.
What it teaches: Master, alive workers, and application id. An application is something you can stop.

Title: Open the Store Rollup
What the shift is: Submit store-rollup the QuickBite way: 2 executors, one core and 512m each, event log on, and a cap so it cannot take every core. Do not change sales-nightly or dispatch-stream. The ticket asks for 2g executors. Do not use it.
What it teaches: A production submit is a shape, not a name. The ticket template can be wrong.

Title: Store Rollup Is on One Worker
What the shift is: store-rollup's two executors are both on worker-0, because that worker was given both cores, and it is patched tonight. Set every worker back to one core and restart store-rollup so the executors land on two workers. Do not give the other workers two cores.
What it teaches: Executors packed on one worker die with that worker. They do not move until the app is placed again.

Title: Worker 2 Left the Cluster
What the shift is: dispatch-stream is still running, but worker-2 is stopped, so the app is an executor short. Start that worker and wait until the executor is back. Leave the driver up.
What it teaches: A stopped worker is lost capacity, not a failed job. Do not resubmit the app.

Title: Store Rollup Is Not Starting
What the shift is: store-rollup is waiting and will not run until both executors are up. worker-1 is stopped, so only one can be placed. A note says to set the executor count to one so the job starts. Do not. Start worker-1 and leave the count at two.
What it teaches: The executor count is the rule. Dropping it makes the job look started, and the next worker loss stops the job.

Title: Disk Full on Worker 1
What the shift is: worker-1 keeps dropping executors because its local directory is full. scratch, left over from an incident, is almost all of the bytes, and worker cleanup was left off so dead application files are kept forever. Free the disk. Leave the dispatch checkpoint and the warehouse output alone.
What it teaches: A full local directory drops executors. Cleanup only helps once leftover files can be deleted.

Title: The Nightly History Was Cleaned
What the shift is: sales-nightly has disappeared from the history server. The cleaner was set to one hour, so that run's event log is gone. Put the cleaner back to 7 days, and set the cluster default so a long-running app rolls its event log. Do not resubmit sales-nightly.
What it teaches: The history cleaner is retention for the UI. Rolling keeps a long-running app from one file growing without limit. You cannot recreate an event log the cleaner already removed.

Title: One Query of Dispatch Is Behind
What the shift is: dispatch-stream is behind on the restaurant-prep query only. The rider-zone query is caught up. The prep query is stuck. Restart the application. The lag has to fall because it reads, not because the checkpoint is deleted.
What it teaches: A stuck query is not a slow cluster. A new checkpoint hides the unread input.

Title: Put the Dispatch Checkpoint Back
What the shift is: During the last incident someone started restaurant-prep from the latest file. The input is still there. Stop the app, put the checkpoint back to the copy in the ticket, and start it again. Do not start from the beginning.
What it teaches: The checkpoint is the read position. Latest skips the backlog. Earliest replays days that were not asked for.

Title: Dispatch Incident
What the shift is: restaurant-prep is behind, and the worker holding its executor has a full local disk, so those batches fail. The other query is fine. Free the disk, or stop that worker so a worker with room takes the executor. The query has to read forward. Do not delete the checkpoint, and do not drop the executor count to one.
What it teaches: One incident can be a full disk and a stuck query at once. The shortcuts in the ticket are the wrong ones.

Title: Apply the Store Rollup Request
What the shift is: A request file for store-rollup is in the ticket. Finish the checker so it submits the job to the lab 01 shape and does not touch the applications already running.
What it teaches: Submits go through a tool that knows the company rules.

Title: Refuse the Bad Template
What the shift is: The same checker is handed a 2g executor and a request for every core. It must refuse and leave the cluster unchanged.
What it teaches: The tool fails closed. A bad request starts nothing.

Title: Lag Report for Dispatch Stream
What the shift is: Ship a small command that prints lag per query and exits non-zero when any dispatch-stream query is over the limit in the ticket.
What it teaches: The on-call check for lag is a tool, not a memory of the UI.

Title: Worker Report
What the shift is: Ship a report that lists workers that are not alive
What it teaches: and applications with fewer executors running than they requested. A healthy cluster prints nothing and exits clean.
Cluster: The on-call check for a missing worker is the same kind of tool.

Title: Caps from the Service Template
What the shift is: Apply the template. dispatch-stream may use one core. store-rollup may use one core. A submit that asks for every core is denied.
What it teaches: A core cap is a template, not a one-off flag. This cluster has no queues. The cap is the share.

Title: Cap the Replay
What the shift is: One application is using every core
What it teaches: so dispatch-stream cannot replace an executor. Cap that application at one core. Leave dispatch-stream running.
Cluster: A cap is how the platform stops one job from taking the cluster.

Title: Detect Submit Drift
What the shift is: The desired file says store-rollup has two 512m executors and the event log on. The running app has one 2g executor and no event log. The tool prints the difference and does not change anything.
What it teaches: Seeing drift and fixing drift are separate.

Title: Reconcile Store Rollup
What the shift is: Same drift as the previous lab. The tool resubmits from the file and waits until both executors are running.
What it teaches: The control plane can repair a job back to the file.

Title: Drain Helper
What the shift is: A command moves executors off one worker, stops it, and leaves dispatch-stream running at its full executor count. The checkpoint stays. The executor count is not lowered to make the drain look done.
What it teaches: A drain is a tool with the same safety rules as the admin labs.

Title: Job Request API
What the shift is: A small local API other teams call to run a job. It uses the same rules as the bad-template lab. A bad body is rejected. A good body submits the job.
What it teaches: Other teams should not need spark-submit to ask for a job.

Title: Submit Defaults
What the shift is: A sample submit has the event log off and dynamic allocation on. This cluster has no shuffle service. Bring the submit to the platform default and show the job still finishes.
What it teaches: Safe submit defaults are a platform standard. Dynamic allocation without a shuffle service drops shuffle data.

Title: History Is Pointing at the Wrong Directory
What the shift is: sales-nightly finished and its event log is on disk. The history server is up and pointed at an empty directory, so the run is not in the UI. Point it at the real directory. The workers stay as they are.
What it teaches: The history server only reads the event log. A blank UI can be the wrong directory, not a lost job.

Title: Dead-Letter Convention
What the shift is: One bad file stalls restaurant-prep. Copy it to the dead-letter path with the original name, then let the query commit past it.
What it teaches: The platform's rule for a bad file, so the rest of the input can move.

Title: Team Prefixes
What the shift is: New applications must be named sales., dispatch., or restaurant. A request for a name outside those prefixes is rejected.
What it teaches: Names are how many teams share one cluster without colliding.

Title: Noisy Neighbor
What the shift is: The backfill is using every core and dispatch-stream is falling behind. The core cap is the fix
What it teaches: and the lag then drains.
Cluster: One job can make the cluster look slow. The cap is the platform's answer.

Title: Trust Store
What the shift is: spark-submit fails the handshake. The master certificate is fine. The trust store in the ticket is the current one. Swap it in and the submit succeeds.
What it teaches: A failed handshake can be the client's trust store, not a down master.

Title: Denied Submit in the Audit Log
What the shift is: After the request API, a rejected submit shows up with the caller and the application name.
What it teaches: A denial the platform cannot see in a log is not finished.

Title: Copy the Sales Summary to the Partner Cluster
What the shift is: A second small cluster is the partner feed. The sales summary written here is readable there once the copy is running.
What it teaches: Some readers are outside this cluster. The platform runs the copy.

Title: Executor Budget
What the shift is: A request for 200 executors is over this cluster's budget. Reject it. A request for 2 is allowed.
What it teaches: Executor count is capacity, and the platform holds the budget.

Title: Pipeline Tag on Every Submit
What the shift is: Every application carries a pipeline tag. The checker fails the submit that omitted it and passes once that submit is fixed.
What it teaches: A required tag is a platform rule on the submit, not a worker setting.

Title: One Task Is Stuck on Worker 0
What the shift is: Almost all of the stage time is one task on worker-0
What it teaches: and speculation is off. Turn speculation on for that job. Do not drop the input.
Cluster: A slow stage can be one stuck task. Speculation runs a second copy.

Title: The New Worker Is Empty
What the shift is: A fourth worker is in the cluster and holds no executors. Spread store-rollup onto it and wait until an executor is running there.
What it teaches: A new worker is unused until an application is placed again.

Title: Patch One Worker
What the shift is: Take one worker out on purpose, show dispatch-stream still runs, start it again, and wait until the executor count is back.
What it teaches: A planned restart is one worker at a time, with the executor count held.

Title: Jobs Are Calling the Wrong Master
What the shift is: The shell can see the cluster. The apps were handed an address that only works on the master itself. Fix the address clients are given.
What it teaches: The address a job uses has to be reachable from the driver.

Title: The Shuffle Service Is Refusing Fetches
What the shift is: Jobs look fine on the master. Dynamic allocation is on, and tasks fail fetching shuffle from an executor that already went away. The shuffle service is not running. Start it. Do not delete the checkpoint.
What it teaches: A task can fail beside the workers. The shuffle service is what lets an executor go away without taking its map output with it.
